after: ## Issues at global, national and local level
alt: Rings show media issues locally (local papers closing, rumours in messaging groups), nationally (funding public service broadcasters, minority languages on air) and globally (false information crossing borders, journalists’ safety). Below, definitions of misinformation, disinformation and media literacy.
caption: Media issues can be found at every level, from a local paper to global press freedom.

alt: Seven groups around a media issue, each with its concern and reason: journalists, media owners, governments, advertisers, technology platforms, audiences and minority-language communities. Below, Article 19 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights is used to support both less regulation and more support for independent media.
caption: Ask who gains, who loses and who decides; the same source can back opposite views.

alt: A chain: advertising money moves online, so papers have less income, so reporters are cut, so fewer council meetings and courts are reported. Other causes are falling print sales and merged titles; further consequences are less checking of local decisions and more reliance on unverified posts.
caption: Linked steps show how one change leads to the next.

alt: McCombs and Shaw (1972) found that the issues undecided voters in Chapel Hill rated most important during the 1968 US presidential campaign closely matched the issues the media covered most. Three limitations: a link is not cause, the sample was one town, and it predates online news.
caption: A strong link is still not proof of cause.

alt: A fictional broadcaster, VNB, claims 9 in 10 viewers trust it and that it is the country’s most trusted source. The evidence covers only its own viewers, so the claim jumps to a national comparison it never makes. Four steps evaluate it: vested interest, a sample that favours VNB, overstated wording, and the need for a random national sample.
caption: Use details from the source; “it is biased” on its own earns little.

alt: Two columns. Australia passed its News Media Bargaining Code in 2021; Facebook briefly blocked news in February 2021, then signed deals, and in 2024 Meta said it would not renew them. Canada’s Online News Act received Royal Assent on 22 June 2023; Meta ended news on its platforms there in August 2023, while Google agreed C$100 million a year. Results: new money for some news organisations, but reduced access to news on one platform.
caption: A law can bring money to news and also cut access to it.

alt: A table of four actions with a strength and a weakness: media literacy teaching, independent fact-checking, public funding for public service or local media, and community action. Below, five questions to judge any action: how well it would work, cost, who gains, who loses and whether it could be done.
caption: Each action trades speed, reach, cost and independence differently.

after: ## Individual Report and Team Project ideas
alt: Three rows link a local media issue to an action and a measure: a printed notice sheet for residents who miss online council news, measured by a survey; a translated message board for families, measured by replies to school events; and a check-before-you-share session, measured by a quiz.
caption: Each project pairs a local communication gap with a measurable fix.
